speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Locarno treaty does
not became effective until after Germany has been admitted to the League of Nations. If we wait for another week or two to discuss the question at the regular time, I do not think the interests of any parties concerned will suffer. I may say to my hon. friend that it has been suggested that the subject of the Locarno agreement might properly come up for discussion when we are taking up the estimates relating to External Affairs, and I hope to bring on those estimates very shortly after we conclude with the budget resolutions.

I understand that the
next meeting of the league will not take place until next September. I hope the Prime Minister will not keep us here till then.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am at one with my hon. friend in the hope that the session is drawing to a close.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for East
Lamb ton (Mr. Armstrong) expressed a desire to speak on this item. I am not sure whether any other hon. gentlemen wish to speak on it or not. I suggest that we might clear the slate, with the understanding that the hon. member can speak on another item.
Item stands.

3. Resolved, that schedule B to the Customs tariff, 1907, as amended by chapter thirty-eight of the statutes of 1924, be further amended by striking thereout item 1031, the enumeration of goods, and the rate of drawback to the said item and to provide that the following items, enumerations and rates of drawback of customs duties be inserted in said schedule B:- Customs tariff-1050. Sugar, when used in the manufacture of loganberry wine. Provided that drawback shall not be payable in respect of any raw sugar produced in a British country-payable as drawback 99 per cent.

Sir HENRY DRAY'TON: What is the change there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a new item to permit the use of sugar in the manufacture of loganberry wine.
Is that a new industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not a new industry, but they claim they have not been given the same privileges as the other wine-makers throughout Canada. This places them in the same position as the others.
Mr, ROGERS: Is there anything else in the loganberry wine except sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You will have to ask somebody from British Columbia.
Yes, the finest berries in the world.
On account of the noise in the chamber it is impossible for us in this section of the House to hear anything that is being said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. members will have to refrain from talking.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1051. Artificial silk tops and waste or artificial fibre silk tops and waste enumerated in tariff item 583A, when further manufactured after the 31st day of December, 1925, and prior to the 1st day of January, 1928-payable as drawback 80 per cent.
What is the change here?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is extending the privilege they have had for some years for the further period of two years only. The article is not made in Canada. It is used in Canadian mills for making wool.
I have not heard one word the minister has uttered.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will speak more loudly.
If it is impossible for the minister to make himself heard where he is sitting, perhaps the Minister of National Defence will permit him to take his seat, and then we might all hear.

This item is under tariff number 583A. I understand this matter was dealt with during the last several sessions of parliament. The article mentioned herein, in regard to which this item is submitted, is now being manufactured at Cornwall, and yet the minister wants to extend this provision for a longer period. Is that the wish of the people who originally bad this item put on the statute book?

Ways and Means-Drawbacks

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The people to whom this was originally given have been consulted, and they offered no objection to this extension. My hon. friend will observe that it refers to waste, and they have not made any of this waste yet.

This item is to be taken into consideration along with the other item. Just as soon as they begin to manufacture they will have waste. They started to manufacture only a few months before the first of January, and they could not be expected to have waste. If we change that item now, what becomes of them during the next six months or a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is extended for two years only and it has been represented that the people interested have no objection.
Reverting to item 1050, in connection with loganberry wine, is the condition in that item, with reference to sugar produced in British countries, the same as that which applies to grape wine?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same condition.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1052. Artificial silk yarns or filaments enumerated in tariff item 5S3aa, imported prior to the 1st day of January, 1926, when further manufactured prior to the 1st day of January 1927-payable as drawback 80 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is to permit them to use the stock on hand on the 1st of January, in order to give them a year to clean up.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1053. Cellulose acetate in powdered form imported after the thirtieth day of April, 1927, and prior to the first day of November, 1927, when imported by manufacturers and further manufactured in their own factories before the first day of December, 1927-payable as drawback 99 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is for a new industry, a very large one, which it is proposed to establish at Drummondville, and this is given them for a six months' period until they get started.
Are there any other industries of this kind in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is a new industry. It is represented to us that it is different from any of the other industries.

What is the difference between this industry and the one established at Cornwall? They are both manufacturing artificial silk are they not; both products are made by practically the same process, out of pulp, and both in exactly the same way, or as nearly as possible in the same way.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been represented to us by the promoters that in many respects they are different products.
What do the gentlemen who are not the promoters but are the beneficiaries under the last tariff say with regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am interested in getting new industries in the country. It is represented that this concern will make a capital investment of $10,000,000.

Is the minister not at all interested in keeping faith with the gentlemen with whom he made arrangement a year ago? The minister made an arrangement a year ago with another firm already established, and now by this tariff he takes off this duty-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
-by permitting this cellulose acetate to be brought in. This acetate is the basis of artificial silk. The cost of cellulose acetate is 75 per cent of the cost of artificial silk.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will observe that this is only for a period of six months. The department has had no objection from the other industries which have been established.

Is it not true that, in the case of the industry established in Cornwall the permission to import or to secure the drawback on cellulose acetate was extended until they had installed the necessary plant and machinery to make their own cellulose acetate; that in the period so fixed in previous legislation they expended the capital, put in their own plant and are now successfully making cellulose acetate? The minister extends this privilege to a sister concern, a new concern, as he says, but does he not realize the injustice he is doing to the concern established a couple of years ago which acted in perfectly good faith?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The business is so large that the older concern is not able to supply the requirements of the industry. I repeat that they have no objections.
Is it intended to limit thi3 strictly to six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what the item says.

The minister
says that they have no objections. Has he had any correspondence with that company?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have had correspondence, but they have offered no serious objections.

Ways and Means-Drawbacks

The minister
uses the word " serious " now. Will he read some of the correspondence so as to let us see whether the objection is serious or not? The minister said a moment ago that he had no objection from this company upon whom this duty was levied in this country. Now he tells us that there is no serious objection. It is only fair that the minister who has had correspondence with these people should place it before the House so that we may know whether the objection is serious or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. Surely
the minister is going to make some statement in reference to the matter. What does he mean by "serious"? Is he serious himself? It is only fair to the committee that he should put on record the letter showing whether there are any objections or not. The truth of the matter is that this House imposed a duty on an article so that a firm might make it in this country. That duty came into effect on the first January of this year and this firm has had three months and fifteen days of protection. Now the bars are let down for another company. It does not make any difference whether this other company is large or small, the arrangement was made; it was on the faith of the government that this company, one of the best in the world, came here from England. They have established themselves in this country on the basis laid down by this government, on the promise of a duty, and this government left them with three months and fifteen days of that protection. Now they have practically taken it off in favour of another company.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend moves to have the correspondence brought down there will be no objection whatever. I repeat: This is only for a period of six months in order that this company may establish itself. It represents to us that the product is not the same; but even if we admit for a moment that the product is the same, does my hon. friend argue that for all time Canada is going to give a monopoly to one industry?

I never argued any such thing. I say that when a duty is imposed on an article, anyone can come in and take advantage of the duty the same as anyone else. What right has the minister to take the protection away from one firm and give another the benefit of it? That is what is being done by this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are giving this only for a period of six months and we are giving to this concern concessions similar to those given to the other.

But the minister made an arrangement with another firm that the duty would come into effect on a certain day. Instead of carrying out that arrangement, the minister says that they are doing this only for six months. In other words the minister says that the government are justified in breaking their word for six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Has my hon. friend in his possession correspondence from the company complaining in this regard?

The company
did not correspond with me. The minister has the correspondence.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member speaking on behalf of the company? He seems to be very much exercised over the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They take the same attitude
to-day.

They take the same attitude to-day? How do we know that? Why should the minister refuse to put the correspondence on the table and let us see for ourselves? For my part I do not agree with the minister at all that they take the same attitude. However, the result was that the time was extended and the duty was to take effect on January 1 last. With these budget resolutions now before us, however, we find that these people have had only three months and fifteen days of protection. Another firm comes along and the minister says, "Oh, well, we have somebody big to attend to now. We have to help them." Why should the minister help someone else at the expense of the people who are already here and with whom he has made an arrangement? The thing is absurd; it is unreasonable; and it is eminently unjust. It is something that is not at all creditable to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend apparently
has not read the resolution. He says that they have had only three months' protection. If he reads the resolution he will observe that its provisions will begin to take effect only on April 30. 1927. and will continue in force until November. 1927. Now I confess at once, after listening to my hon. friend, that I have some doubts as to whether he represents the views of this company or not. If he does, then the representative of the Manufacturers' Association in Ottawa, v/ho called upon the minister, has misrepresented the situation, for he said to mg that these people offered no objection and did not regard the change as serious.

This is my
answer to that, statement:	I do not see why
the minister should want to hold someone else responsible now. Why should he drag somebody else into the proposition? That is very much in line with his statement last night, which in my opinion was very much beside the point, to the effect that another gentleman had camped on his doorstep on behalf of some other firm. It seems to me the Minister would do well to leave out such irrelevancies, especially as I understand that he has had correspondence with these people. If he has had such correspondence in reference to this matter, why should he not put it on the table?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The correspondence of the
Department of Finance is not carried around by the minister or anybody else. If the hon. member moves for a return I will table it.

Ways and Means-Drawbacks

I will ask the
minister to allow the matter to stand for the time being until the correspondence is tabled.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I cannot let it stand.

I confess I am at a loss
to imagine why the minister should refuse the request of the hon. member for Lincoln that this matter be allowed to stand pending the return of the correspondence. If the minister is acting in good faith, as I beileve he is, I see no reason why he should object to bringing down the correspondence before the item is disposed of, in view of the fact that the hon. member makes rather serious charges against him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My reason for not holding
over the item is the fact that this House comprises 245 members and the hon. member for Lincoln is only one individual. I do not propose to hold up the rest of the House on his account. -

Let me point out to the
minister that the hon. member for Lincoln, is one of 116 members sitting around him, the vast majority of whom most probably share his views. He is therefore not alone in this matter. Apparently, if we are to draw any conclusion from this incident, it is this-that the Minister of Finance will enter into an argeement with some corporation from England to establish an industry in this country and, having given them a solemn undertaking to protect them for a certain length of time, he will go back on his word after a very brief interval. In other words, the government again break faith with those to whom they have pledged themselves to carry out some undertaking.
That is not so.
Who says it is not so?
Read the resolution.

I know quite rvell what
the resolution contains. But does it make any difference that there is a slight change in the time specified in the resolution? The fact is that the minister is violating his agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The representative of the
Manufacturers' Association has said that the company offers no objection.

But the representative of
that association is not the representative of the company, and it is the company with whom the minister dealt.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend speak
for the company?

No; nor do I know the
company at all. But I have heard this dis. cussion, and I have heard the member for Lincoln make a statement which the minister so far has not denied, that an agreement was entered into with the company to. give them protection until they were well established. And now the minister comes along, when another company comes on the scene, and proposes to ignore his agreement, in order that this other company may be established in Quebec. That is the situation as it is represented to the minister now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend opposed
to industries being established in Quebec?

No; I am as good a friend of Quebec as the minister is. The minister will not question that. I have never had anything against Quebec. I do believe, however, in living up to one's agreements; I believe in keeping faith with the industries of Ontario as well as with those of Quebec. Now, are we to draw the conclusion from the minister's attitude in this matter that no corporation that proposes to set up in this country maj'' place confidence in this government for any longer period than three and a half months? Are we to assume that in so short a time this government will set aside an agreement it makes with such a corporation for the reason that some other firm wishes to establish an industry? It does not seem to me that we shall attract many capitalists if we pursue such a policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before the item passes I want to clear up this matter. We never agreed with any company. Neither this government nor the preceding nor any other government ever undertook to give the company a monopoly of business for all time, and the company recognize this fact, because through the representative of the Manufacturers' Association they have said that they offer no objection to the item. I want to know now whether my hon. friend from Lincoln and my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) are speaking on behalf of the company?

I cannot speak for the
hon. member for Lincoln, but I have already told the minister that I do not even know the name of the company. But I have heard the matter discussed this afternoon and I heard, the hon. member for Lincoln make a reasonable request, that the minister allow the item to stand over until to-night and table the correspondence in the meantime. Why cannot the minister let the item stand? We

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
shall not get through these resolutions tonight, and to my mind the minister is taking a very unreasonable and unfair stand in this matter.

The minister
again implies that I am acting for the company. Let me assure him, as I have already done, that I am not doing anything of the kind. I am saying, however-I have said it many times before-that in my opinion the minister is not treating these people fairly. He wants to know whether they have complained to me. No. But I understand that they complained to the minister. Now, the minister says the matter is not serious. Well, if that be so why can he not table the correspondence and let us see for ourselves just what it says?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even if they do complain, why should parliament be deprived of the right to change the tariff in any matter?

Parliament is not being
deprived of any right, but we are simply asking that the correspondence 'be brought down.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In regard to tariff matters the House of Commons is supreme.

Undoubtedly.
Parliament is supreme, and the minister is getting his cue from the hon. gentleman alongside him when he makes that statement. But is there a government at all?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

And does that
government make an agreement and then break it in six months? That is what you have done and what you evidently will continue to do.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Governments cannot
make agreements on tariff matters.

The minister
on reflection will, I think, postpone consideration of the item. I fancy he will make headway if he does so. We know nothing of the matter, having had no information regarding it until we came into the House. The minister knows that after some difficulty-I will not expatiate on that point-the member for Lincoln discovered that objections had been made, and he finds now that there has been correspondence on the subject. He wants to have that correspondence brought down, and the minister is willing to bring it down but he proposes to do so at a time when the correspondence can do not the slightest good. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) gets very wrathy and declares that parliament is
supreme. Who is questioning that fact? Who is challenging the right of parliament in any respect? But may I suggest to the Minister of Justice that we on this side constitute a part of parliament and that we too have some rights? We have got at least 116 out of 245, and we propose to exercise those rights. And we are justified in doing so. Now, the only way that parliament-this supreme body -can handle this matter intelligently surely is with the evidence before it. The minister says he has the correspondence and that we can have it after this is all settled. I wonder if the Minister of Justice-	.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Whether this company
likes it or not, in what way does it affect the merits of the proposal?

We might, for example, Mr. Chairmap, know for the first time something about the reasons which are actuating any tariff change; we might, for example, know whether there were any real reasons against it; we might, for example, get to know whether the government are acting on sound reason or without any reason at all. So far as I am concerned. I have absolutely nothing against this item. I am frank to say I know nothing about it. But I do think, Mr. Chairman, we will make better headway if when a request which does seem to me reasonable, a request which flows from what the minister himself says, that he has this corresnon Hence is not lightly turned down. Apparently, from what the minister says, there are some objections to the legislation. I wonder if the Minister of Justice thinks _ we ought to decide the question without knowing anything about the objections, without knowing anything about the merits. There is no doubt as to what these people want. It is a question of the merits they show in their correspondence, that is all. Is not the House entitled to consider the merits one way or the other; and how can they do so without having the facts before them? As I say, I know nothing about this item, but, it does seem to me we will get better results if we deal frankly with each other, and if these objections, whether good or bad, be made known to the House before the House acts.

The Minister of Justice
says that parliament is supreme in these tariff matters; but yesterday when a motion was proposed by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) to raise the tariff on meats to five cents, the Chair ruled that parliament had nothing to do with it, that it was the discretion of the government alone.

Ways and Means-Drawbacks

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is mistaken; that was not the reason at all.

Mr. Chairman, so far as
this industry is concerned which is to be established in the province of Quebec, I am naturally desirous of giving every advantage' to it or to any other new industiy which may be established in that province or in any other province. But the only reason which we have so far before the House for the passing of the item in its present form is that some representative of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, orally or in writing, stated to the Minister of Finance that there is no reasonable objection to it. Now,
I for one, although a Conservative and a protectionist, absolutely refuse, even if the Minister of Finance is willing to do so, to put my conscience and my judgment in the keeping of any representative of the Manufacturers' Association.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree with that. .

I think we are entitled to know if there is any serious objeetion. The minister admits that there is objection, but in his mind it is not serious. Now, many objections have been presented in argument before this House which the minister does not regard as serious-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-but which we regard as very vital, material, relevant and important. Therefore I suggest that in keeping with the usual courtesy of the minister it will assist in passing those items as expeditiously as possible if he does lay before the House the information which he has. The Minister of Justice suggests that there is no ground for inviting the presentation of this correspondence to the House because it does not matter what protest has been made, it will not influence the opinion and judgment of the government. Now I am sure the Minister of Justice does not intend to go that far. He is certainly one of the most courteous of ministers, and he is always more courteous than his suggestion would indicate. I am sure he really does not mean that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A moment of weakness.

Having knowledge of the
objection, the minister does not regard it as very serious or very relevant; but as the question has been raised with regard to its seriousness and relevancy, why not allow the members of this House to judge for themselves, to have the actual facts presented by the correspondence?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I observe that the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is now in his seat and I am prepared to take up item 469b-in view of the very great courtesy with which the hon. member for Lincoln has asked for this.

Mr. Chairman,
I have to thank the minister very heartily for his consideration.
Item stands.
Customs tariff-469b. Machinery a<nd apparatus and parts thereof for use only in producing unrefined oil or fertilizer from shales, not to include motive power of a class or kind made in Canada: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the courtesy which the minister has extended to me in allowing me the few minutes' grace necessary to bring up this matter. The industry which I am speaking for is located in my riding and over S3,000,000 has been invested in it. Thousands of people in the town and adjacent villages are vitally interested in this industry. In the first place, let me say that I have no objection whatever to the item as it stands. I am merely bringing up the subject at this point, this being the only item in which crude petroleum is mentioned. The minister supported the Hon. Mr. Fielding in 1923 in removing the bounty on crude petroleum. At that time there was a bounty of a cent and a half per gallon. This bounty was to offset the removal of the protective tariff. The minister is well aware that every bit of casing, pumps, tubing, rods, valves, and tools of all kinds used in the oil industry have either to be purchased from a protected industry in Canada, or, if that material is brought in from the United States, a duty of from 27J per cent to 30 per cent has to be paid thereon, in addition to sales tax of five per cent, all of which goes into the treasury of this country. So it will readily be seen that it is impossible for the producers to carry on under present conditions, if they have to buy their supplies from industries in this country protected to that extent. The minister has been told this a number of times; delegations have come to Ottawa and placed this matter before him and he has been urged in the strongest possible terms to give some relief to this industry. Last session there was placed before the minister the report of an investigation made by Mr. Hume of the Geological Survey, which showed conclusively that the industry could not carry on under present conditions. I will

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
admit that a great many properties are continuing to operate, but I do not know of one being carried on at a profit. I can safely say that practically every property in that western district is being carried on at a loss, owing to the conditions I have stated.
The minister was urged last year to make an investigation, and he was good enough to do so. He sent his expert, Mr. Russell, who is now before him, to investigate that industry. Mr. Russell spent a considerable time there and, as we thought, made a very fair investigation. He was given every opportunity to investigate every part of the industry; he had statements placed before him of the operation of a number of the large producing companies; they showed their books to him, gave him financial statements, and placed before him conclusive evidence showing that they could not possibly carry on without some form of protection or bounty, or the removal of at least the duty on supplies which they purchase from protected industries. I understand that Mr. Russell made a report upon his return to Ottawa, as was natural. I have asked for that report, which I think is a reasonable request, but unfortunately the minister has not seen fit to bring it down. I am satisfied that if it were placed before parliament it would be seen that Mr. Russell has come to the same conclusion as Mr. Hume, that this industry could not possibly carry on.
I received a letter from the minister a day or so ago asking why the production of crude oil in Canada had materially increased since the reduction of this bounty. I can answer that in this way, that so far as the old districts are concerned the production has decreased. But two or three years ago an important well was drilled by the Imperial Oil Company in the northwest, and that well is responsible for all the extra oil worth mentioning that has been produced in this country. Millions of dollars were spent by the Imperial Oil Company before that well was brought in, and millions of dollars have since been spent by that company and others in trying to bring in another such well. That well is not producing what we call crude oil, but it is oil of a more refined nature, and I am informed that it can be taken from the well and placed right in the motor, while the crude oil produced elsewhere has to be further refined.
These are just some of the things I would like to place before the minister, and I would like to urge that this industry be given some relief. I do not wish to take up the time of the House in going into further details, but I sincerely hope the minister has come to some definite conclusion in regard to this
matter. I looked upon the minister as a fair minded man in years past, when I had the privilege of sitting in the House with him, and I cannot believe that he will continue to keep the producers of crude oil in western Ontario in their present position. I tell him frankly that unless some immediate assistance is given that industry, inside of twelve months it will be in a very much worse condition than it is to-day.

This item deals with
the duty on special machinery connected with the production of oil from shale and the production of fertilizer from oil bear-i p.m. ing-shale. This is a new industry in Canada; at present no such operations are being conducted in a commercial way, and the necessary machinery for this work is not made in Canada. This is therefore an instance where it seems proper that the tariff should allow this expensive and special machinery to be brought into Canada without duty. It will not interfere with any firm or firms making this machinery7 in Canada, because this machinery is not made here. I therefore take this opportunity of approving of the item, because I hope it will lead to the establishment in Canada of these industries, and because it does not interfere, as I have already said, with any manufacturers in Canada who make this special apparatus. So much for that.
I should also like to say a word in reference io the bounty on oil. There was a bounty granted by parliament for a number of years, but two or three years ago it was removed by the previous Minister of Finance. His reason was that there were immediate prospects of there being a large discovery of oil in the northwest of Canada, which, should it occur, would involve the payment of a very heavy sum of money by way of bounty to the owners of these oil wells. At the time it was pointed out in this House that that was a premature decision. While we hoped that the oil would be found, actually it was not found, and it has not been found up to to-day in large quantities. It was also pressed on the minister that the amount of bounty to be paid might be safeguarded by limiting payments to a certain amount of production, to a certain number of barrels from any particular well in a certain time. That would have safeguarded against any great expenditure of the funds of the country. However, that view did not prevail, and with two years' notice the bounty was removed. I would again take this opportunity of stating that I think the bounty was removed prematurely. Actually the oil

No.

They say that they have obtained these pipes and casings from some of the industries in Canada that are protected, but that they do not stand up under the pressure when they go down to great depth, and we have been urged to reduce the duty and make some concessions in order to allow these pipes and casings to come in. It is true that in the older sections the flow of the oil wells has somewhat diminished, but in other sections it has increased, and my predecessor, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, having in mind the advertisements we were reading of the great possibilities of developing gushers overnight, with a great flow of oil, and the danger of the bounty on these gushers bankrupting the treasury, gave notice that the bounty, which had prevailed in Canada for many years, since 1903 or 1904, I think, would be 1\ cents a gallon up to the 30th of June, 1924, and then be reduced to three-quarters of a cent a gallon up to the 30th of June, 1925, when it would be discontinued. Is that due to the

speechtext:

With these figures before us I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, I appeal to my genial friend the former Minister of Finance, would we have been justified in going back to the bounty system?

I know
the minister is well aware of the reason for that increase; he knows quite well that it is due to that one well of which I spoke a few minutes ago, which has been producing four hundred or five hundred barrels of oil a day. He must realize that in the United States the flush production to-day amounts to over two million barrels a day, and this average has been maintained for the past year. The minister must also remember that in the United States, with their flush production, they have no such thing as a sales tax and no such thing as a duty on the materials they have to purchase. He knows perfectly well the reason why the former administration could not touch this question. Everbody knows it. My hon. friend admits it. So we have the principle admitted, Mr. Chairman, that in a proper scientific tariff as you go further up in your processes your tariff increases for the purpose of protecting Canadian labour. I am going to give a few figures just to show how, when you take a jump in the dark and know absolutely nothing of what you are doing, as we have clearly shown the government acted, disastrous results are bound to follow. I can take any single basic material going into this manufacture and show that my hon. friend has absolutely violated the principle that he upholds.
My hon. friend is speaking seriously?
Oh, yes.

Why does he have such
a nice smile on his face all the time when he says that?

I am quite sure my hon. friend's suggestion is a great help to the debate. But does he think it is possible for me to portray in my face just what I feel when I see mirrored before me such appalling ignorance in dealing with this subject? I cannot do it. The position is laughable.
I said smiling.

Well, it is really laughable to think that people who are supposed to have serious responsibilities placed upon them-other than the one responsibility of hanging on to office .as best they may- would with the information before them take the step which is here taken. It is sad, but at the same time it is laughable. Now then, I am going to take cotton. The raw material is of course free. When it gets to cotton yarn the tariff is 25 per cent; cotton cloth and yarn the same; cotton cloth, not dyed, 25 per cent; cotton cloth dyed, 32i per cent. Rubber-coated cloth, 30 per cent; top material 30 per cent. These items all go into tops, and there is a good deal more Canadian labour in the tops than there is in the cotton cloth dyed, which is given to-day a duty of 32i per cent, while tops are given a duty of 20 per cent. That is how it works out.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I notice my hon. friend is well posted on the cotton trade. Will he tell me what percentage of a dollar's worth of cotton is labour?

Suppose we take something else. Suppose we take iron. That is part of your materials again. The free iron ore you convert into pig iron. Then there is a duty of $2.50 per ton. Then you are going to do something with this iron in connection with your cars. You have to have wheel hubs and wheels. Your wheel hubs are metal. There is a 30 per cent duty on the wheel hub, which the Canadian manufacturer has to pay. The next thing you have in connection with your iron is malleable castings which you put into your axles. When it takes the form of malleable castings it gets a protection of 271 per cent. It goes a little bit further and becomes rear axle housings-a little more Canadian labour in that, and the duty then becomes 30 per cent. It goes on and becomes a rear axle- a bit more Canadian labour in that, if they are made here-and it gets a protection of 35 per cent, while the protection to the whole automobile is put at 20 per cent, with infinitely more Canadian labour upon it.

On iron and steel billets the duty is $2.50 a ton, but when rolled into alloyed steel the duty is twelve and a half per cent. The desire and the policy of the government is not to injure the manufacturers of parts, but to compel the manufacturers of

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a good deal in what my hon. friend says, that because of the war conditions and the necessity for revenue, with the government groping about to find that revenue, we imposed the excise tax and sales tax on cars. But my hon. friend will notice, if he looks at this year's estimates, that we have to correct some of his own troubles in the matter of taxes. It is all costing money; no one knows better than does my hon. friend that it is not so easy to fix up a tariff to satisfy every person. My hon. friend says the Canadian tariff has many inequalities, and I think he is absolutely right.
I quite agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But he carried on an investigation throughout all Canada; he must have looked into the matter pretty carefully, and he had ample opportunity at the time to correct some of these inequalities, but he said a moment ago that he could not do it. And why? Because it is hard; it is dangerous to start changing tariffs, but this government has had the courage to do so, and I think we are receiving the support and approval of the Canadian people.

I think the
Canadian people to-day would very much rather see this question put upon a fair and proper basis. My hon. friend knows very
well why, at the end of that former investigation, nothing could be done. Every hon. gentleman knows that having regard to the United States market and to the invasion of our markets by the United States, this matter had to be looked after very carefully with especial regard to that nation. Everyone knows that at that time taxes which were then temporary, and which bore very heavily upon our people, were in effect in the United States. These were at the balancing point as to whether they should be repealed or should become permanent, and we were told that if we took any action we might perhaps provide an excuse for making those taxes permanent. We therefore held our hand, and whether we were right or wrong, everyone knows why that was done. They know very well we did not do it for any dishonest political purpose; we did not do it for the purpose of catching votes in this House.

My hon. friend who has just taken his seat has used as a very strong argument against the reduction of the duty on automobiles the fact that on all the automobiles made and purchased in Canada the government received $207 in taxes. There is no doubt that the Dominion government did receive approximately that amount on every car produced and consumed in Canada, but my hon. friend did not say that that amount included excise and sales taxes.
My hon. friend is wrong; he could not have listened to me. 1 did say that the duties amounted to about $10,000,000, and the excise and sales taxes to about $7,000,000.
But my hon. friend did not say how much of the $207 was made up by each tax.

I gave the
figures; my hon. friend was not paying attention. The duties amounted to approximately $10.000,000 and. the sales taxes to about $7,400,000.

So that almost fifty per cent of the taxes collected, according to my hon. friend's statement, were collected in

excise and sales taxes. On every car imported from the United States the same amount of sales and excise tax was imposed. This government has a double duty to perform. It must live u,p to the obligations of the Dominion of Canada and honourably pay the interest upon the debt incurred during the recent world war for the benefit of civilization. That can only be done by imposing taxes. The second duty of this government is to make the cost of every commodity required in this country as low to the Canadian consumer as possible. It might be all very well to follow the suggestion of my hon. friend and reduce the cost of automobiles by removing the excise and sales taxes, but if we do that what happens?
I did not make that suggestion; I merely stated that we should know what we are doing before we start.

My hon. friend said that if we wanted to reduce the price of cars it could be done by reducing the tax. We all know and admit that if we reduced the sales tax and the excise tax we could reduce the price of automobiles without hurting our manufacturers and without hurting those who export their cars to this country, but it is our duty to pay our debts, and it is absolutely necessary to maintain that tax, at least for some time, in order to do so. He said not a
few minutes ago.

On a car which is listed at $31,500 in the United States you will find that the duty at 35 per cent on the list price, plus the excise tax in the United States, amounts to $1,250.73; the sales tax on that car is $241.21. The excise tax on the first $1,200 is $60 and the excise tax on the balance is $362.42, forming a total, leaving aside all freight charges, of $5,414.36. When that same car is imported into Canada, as it is generally imported by subsidiary distributing companies-I am speaking of American cars, not cars manufactured in Canada-the company receives a reduction on the list price of 30 per cent for duty purposes. They pay the duty on $2,450 plus the American excise tax of $73.50, so that the duty is SSS3.40; sales tax at 5 per cent is $170.36, excise tax at 5 per cent is $80, and the excise tax at 10 per cent on the balance over $1,200 is $220.69, making a laid down cost on this side of the line of $3,784.44. When the American manufacturer pays his dealer 20 per cent for selling the car he receives $3,500 less $700. or a net price of $2,800. When he sells that same car in Canada for $5,414.36, he pays in duty and taxes the sum of $1,334,314 and he and the dealer to-gether get the balance of $4,080.02. If the dealer gets the same price for selling the car as the American dealer, or $700, the American manufacturer gets the balance of $3,380.02. In other words he gets for every car he sells in Canada $580 more than he receives for the same car when it is sold in the United States. If the American manufacturer gets an additional profit of $580 I claim the Canadian manufacturer enjoys not only the protection of 35 per cent, but also the additional profit made by the

Any car which costs $3,500

enjoyed on any car because the different cars are not always manufactured with the same quantity of parts purchased in Canada. Sometimes more parts are imported than at other times. For that reason it would be absolutely impossible to give the exact net protection on any particular car.
Further the interests of the different car manufacturers are not all alike. The more parts that are imported for one car and the fewer that are imported for others cause a difference of attitude on the part of these manufacturers. Some want one thing and ,some another. Many of these men came to the Minister of Finance and said that it would be a terrible calamity if a 25 per cent drawback were given on parts imported from the United 'States when at least 50 per cent of the car was manufactured in Canada. There were other part manufacturers who were begging with both hands for that conditional concession. The representations of the different part- makers had to be carefully weighed and the benefit given to the majority.
Some automobile manufacturers asked us for free parts; some asked us to put on the free list certain parts not manufactured in Canada and others stated that they were quite .willing to pay duty upon all imported parts. They did not explain the reason but it is evident that there are a certain number of manufacturing interests in this country who have different views. Their views were all heard, weighed and considered, but in weighing and considering those view's, one thing was not lost sight of, and that was the cost of the finished car to the great consuming public of Canada. So long as these automobile industries are able to carry on, so long as they are able to show a fair profit and increase production, they should not ask for more. The government does not desire to do serious injury to any industry. It has listened to the representations of every one of the automobile manufacturers in Canada and of the great majority of manufacturers of parts in this country, and it has endeavoured to meet their views and wishes.

In case he does not, I may tell him that when I have concluded I shall take my seat and will not. do as an hon. member did a few years ago, when he insisted on keeping the floor without speaking.

When was that?
M'r. BOIVIN: If my hon. friend has a question to ask I shall be glad to endeavour to answer him.

All I wanted was to ask a question. I want to know whether the difference between the price the manufacturer charges abroad and that which the home consumer pays is not equivalent to the drawback allowed under the Customs Act.

The manufacturer sells his car cheaper abroad than he does in Canada because he pays a lower duty on parts imported for use in the cars he exports. If therefore he pays a lower duty on such parts for the cars	sold at	home, he ought	to beable to sell	his	cars	in Canada	at a	lowerprice. There is of course one possible objection in that respect: it may be said that because of these lower duties in the form of a drawback on imported parts we shall wipe out the parts industry entirely. But this argument is of no force inasmuch as the only drawback which the manufacturer gets in connection with	the	cars	he exports	is a	drawback, not on	the	cost	of the car,	but on the
duty paid on American material or parts entering into the manufacture of the car when it is made in Canada. And is it not a fact that there are Canadian wheels and bodies on many cars that are exported? I am glad that my hon. friend and I are agreed on one point-that the more you reduce the duty, the cheaper can the manufacturer sell his car.

As regards the selling
of cars abroad, the reduction in the sales and luxury taxes that must be paid in Canada should be fairly set forth. That is where the difference comes in.

That of course makes a
considerable difference, but in the present debate I do not think the question of the sales and luxury taxes has been taken into

consideration by anyone except the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) who referred to them in order to present what appeared on the surface to be a very good case. The hon. gentleman is an able parliamentarian. He submits his views in convincing language, and I am sorry that any hon. member should reproach him for putting them forward with a smile. He used the argument that $207 is paid to the government on an average, on every car manufactured in Canada, and of that $207 he admitted that about 45 per cent consisted in excise and sales taxes. That 45 per cent does not apply to the car that is exported, in connection with which neither sales nor luxury taxes are collected. I want the committee to understand that for the purposes of my argument I have no intention of introducing the sales and luxury taxes, which after all are taxes imposed upon our own citizens, to meet the obligations of the country. I want to consider the cost of the car in Canada in comparison with the export cost without taking these taxes into account. In my opinion the automobile manufacturers made a grievous mistake when they published the list prices of their cars and included therein the sales tax and the luxury tax. This was unfair to themselves. I am prepared to admit that if the manufacturers in Canada had not included in their list prices the sales and luxury taxes, they would not perhaps be so severely censured for the high cost of cars in this country. They have done so however and it may have been for the purpose of making the buyers of cars forget that they had these taxes to pay. I know that the automobile manufacturers are great friends of the party in power.
Oh, oh.
Is that why the duty was reduced?

We did not consider that
when the tariff was discussed.
That is the trend of the minister's argument.

The tariff was reduced for
a reason which I have already given to the committee and which I shall state again. It was reduced in order to bring down the prices of cars in Canada, and put them within reasonable reach of the consumer.

Without regard to those
employed in the industry.

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
My hon. friend and I agreed a few moments ago that the manufacturers of Canadian cars were selling their exportable surplus at lower prices than they were charging the Canadian consumer.
Because they got a drawback.
Because they got a drawback, yes. Now if instead of a drawback they get permission to import free the parts not manufactured in Canada-
Thereby putting the other factories out of business.
What factories?
The parts factories.

May I ask my hon. friend
how we are going to put any parts factory out of business by admitting duty free into Canada any part not manufactured in this country?

There is no objection to
that.

My hon. friend has no
objection to that? Well, I can assure him that it is not the intention of the government to go a step further. We do not intend to ruin any parts factory in this countiy.

It is enough to ruin the
automobile factories.

We do not intend either
to ruin the automobile factories, and as a matter of fact they will not be ruined. Far from that, the manufacturers will sell their cars at a lower price and on that account will sell more cars, making a bigger profit, increasing production, lessening overhead and paying dividends to their shareholders. That will be the result of this tariff change. Whether the part comes in free or whether it gets the 99 per-cent drawback makes very little difference; in one case or in the other the reduction in tariff is going to be passed on to the Canadian consumer. It is not our desire to ruin any manufacturing -industry. The Minister of Finance and the government have one desire in mind in all the proposals submitted to parliament-to encourage production in Canada, and instead of having merely assembling plants, to have fully equipped plants for the complete manufacture of automobiles and other commodities and so employ more Canadian workmen. That is the reason why while some parts may be placed on the free list other parts will not be; but a drawback of 25 per cent on those parts will be given only upon
condition that the manufacturer applying for the drawback shall prove to the government that more than 40 or 50 per cent Canadian labour and Canadian materials have been incorporated in the car.
In the car or in the parts?
In the car or in its component parts.

There is quite a distinction. Take the case of a man making a part, and that part goes into a car, how is he to prove that the car contains 50 per cent Canadian labour and materials? If it read ''50 per cent of Canadian-made parts" it would be clear.

A few moments ago I stated that in the case of cars exported in which Canadian bodies, Canadian wheels, Canadian springs and other Canadian parts were used, the manufacturer exporting will get a drawback of 99 per cent on everything American whether imported direct by himself or by the maker of the parts sold to him to be embodied in the completed car. The 25 per cent drawback which is to be granted by the government under another item of the tariff will be administered in absolutely the same way. That is, if the Canadian car manufacturer buys a part from a Canadian parts manufacturer, he will get a credit of 50 per cent for the Canadian labour and materials in that part.

My hon. friend
I think has cleaned it all up. Take, for example, rims. As my hon. friend knows, we have not the steel in this country for the manufacture of rims, therefore we have to import the rims which are used by our wheel manufacturers. For the purpose of administration, will my hon. friend say that if the Canadian automobile manufacturer buys his wheels from a Canadian wheel manufacturer, notwithstanding the fact that the rims had to be imported from the United States, those wheels will be looked upon as a Canadian product? I so understood from my hon. friend's statement.

Then I do not think my
hon. friend understood me exactly. I said that everything Canadian in those wheels would be considered as part of the 50 per cent of Canadian manufacture and materials contained in the car. It is absolutely the same as the regulation that applies to export at the present time. If those wheels are embodied in a car which goes to a foreign country, a drawback is paid upon the duties paid in respect of all parts included in the car.
Ways and Means-Drawbacks

In the case of
the wheel it would be the duty on the rim?

The duty on the rim would be considered to be duty paid by the Canadian manufacturer of the Canadian content in the car. The drawback of course would not be on the full cost of the wheel; it would be 25 per cent of the duty paid on the rim when imported.
It is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if we might not pass this item which we have been considering all the afternoon.
We are really discussing both items.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had intended before six o'clock to make a statement of certain amendments so that hon. members might have an opportunity to consider them. On 438b I propose to offer as an amendment after the word, "only", the words, "n.o.p., valued at retail when new."
That is new cars of a retail value of $1,200?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That applies to cars of $1,200 and over when new. To that item we shall also add what has been added to the other items, "chassis for motor vehicles specified in this item."
Then there is another item:
Customs tariff-438c. Tops, wheels and bodies, n.o.p., for motor vehicles enumerated in tariff items 438a and 438b: British preferential tariff, 20 per cent; intermediate tariff, 37J per cent; general tariff, 30 per cent.
That is to make them the same rate as the others, and when the discount comes off it will equalize them. They will get the 25 per cent rebate.
I was glad during the discussion this afternoon to find my hon. friend from West York and myself were in agreement, as we oftentimes are. He argued at considerable length that there were many materials that were not manufactured in Canada upon which duty was paid. A new item will be introduced placing on the free list a long list of items, some of which were mentioned by my hon. friend this afternoon, with the safeguarding clause, "of a class or kind not manufactured in Canada."
Has my hon. friend copies of those resolutions?
What will be the rate there?
Free. I think you should read them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The usual thing, Mr. Chairman, is to supply members with copies of such changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I expected my hon. friend would make that statement. I have read Hansard containing his budget, and I would advise him during the dinner hour to refer to it. He will find that he brought down about three pages of changes.
Everyone knew about them, and Mr. Fielding had copies. We made lots of changes in committee, but we had the idea that "parliament was supreme".

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Hear, hear. My hon. friend is becoming converted.
