Customs	tariff-438a. Automobiles and motor
vehicles of all kinds, n.o.p.: British preferential tariff, 15 per cent; intermediate tariff, 25 per cent; general tariff, 27£ per cent.

I notice that the Minister of Customs is not in his place, but he made some statement this- afternoon in respect to which I should like some information. Probably the Minister of Finance can supply it. The Minister of Customs made the definite statement that Canadian made automobiles were being sold in other countries cheaper than in Canada, excluding the sales tax and the drawback. I would ask the Minister of Finance, in the absence of the Minister of Customs, to give us details in that regard. This is a very important question, to my mind, because it is one in which the consuming public are vitally interested. If it is true, the public should know it; if it is not true, I do not think a wrong impression should go out.

Ways and Means-Drawbacks

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Customs will be in, I imagine, before we get through with the next item. He has the papers with him, and I am sure he would not have made that statement had he not known it to be true. Does my hon. friend say it is not true?

I do not believe it is true. I do not see how it could be possible for a Canadian manufacturer to send an automobile to England, pay the duty on it, and sell it over there cheaper than it would be sold in this country. I am only asking for information, because I think this is a question on which the people of this country should know the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That statement is not limited to automobiles. We have heard it frequently made in this House regarding other commodities. My hon. friend has been here almost as many years as myself, and he must have heard that argument applied to other goods.
But I have never had any proof that it is true.
The allegation has been made in reference to agricultural implements especially, and it has never been proved. It was always denied.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And in regard to flour.
The hon. minister knows more about flour than I do. He probably knows how it is done.
It has often been stated that flour manufactured in Canada is sold more cheaply in other countries than in Canada, and just as a matter of information I should like to know if that is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have heard the statement.
I have heard the statement too, but I want to know if it is true.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is entirely out of order, and I would ask you to try to keep this debate to the point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is no further discussion of item 438a we might pass on to the next, on which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario cpuld ask his question.
We have been discussing this matter at large, and I think we might as well discuss this item and 438b together, because the subject matter is about the same.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Then I will read 438b as proposed to be amended:
Customs tariff-43Sb. Automobiles for conveying passengers only, n.o.p., valued at retail, when new, with standard equipment complete at not more than twelve hundred dollars each; motor cars or motor trucks (not for railways or tramways) for carrying goods only'; motor cycles; chassis for motor vehicles specified in this item: British preferential tariff, 124 per cent; intermediate tariff, 171 per cent; general tariff, 20 per cent.
The new item 438c reads:
Customs tariff-438c. Tops, wheels, and bodies, n.o.p., for motor vehicles enumerated in tariff items 438a and 438b: British preferential tariff, 20 per cent; intermediate tariff, 27J per cent; general tariff, 30 per cent,	!
I think, Mr. Chairman, we should discuss the two main automobile items together, and deal with 438c when we reach it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so.
Would the minister explain what he means by that phrase in 438b, "valued at retail when new"?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This applies to automobiles
where the duty is 20 per cent. As every hon. member knows, there are men who sit up nights planning how they may beat governments and customs house officers, and it was represented to us that a car coming under the 274 per cent rate might be run around for two days and then represented to the customs as not a new car, and that it should be allowed to come in under a lower valuation.
This is just taken at the retail price?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I have been
waiting for the Minister of Customs to come into the chamber; he gave us a very interesting illustration of how the Canadian manufacturer exploited the tariff by using the goods of the American exporter here instead of the Canadian product. It was very interesting, but not at all illuminative of the point. Perhaps we can get a case where we are dealing not with an importer of American goods, some agent here who, through the tariff, is enabled to get ahead of the Canadian public, but with a Canadian manufacturer who is doing what the government have alleged, although I do not think they meant it, they have done; that is, exploit the Canadian people. It would be so much better if we could have an illustration of the charge made. The figures given by the Minister of Customs may be absolutely right, but they have noth-

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
ing to do with the case. The question here is whether or not the Canadian manufacturer was exploiting the tariff; I do not know whether he was, but the statement was made, and illustrating that statement we have something the American importer is doing. I would suggest that if the government really has anything, they should let us have it.

According to
the figures given by the Minister of Customs an American manufacturer of cars provides a car at an American list price of $3,500. He is allowed to discount that price in here, as the minister says, by means of a fake company. I would like to know why the minister and others are not preventing this fake business. Whose business is it to look after that sort of thing? Just look at the figures; it seems to me there is something more than smuggling that needs to be taken care of in this country, if those figures are correct. A car valued at $3,500 is discounted to bring it down to $2,800; it pays duty into this country and is sold at $5,400. That, on the face of it, shows incompetency on the part of the customs, if nothing else. That illustration is provided to show that the Canadian manufacturer is doing the same thing, but does it explain it? No. But the minister says the Canadian manufacturer is allowed to compete with that sort of thing and does not compete with it; he is allowed to charge the same price because the other man does it. That is the lamest argument I ever heard of, and I would like to hear the Minister of Customs explain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I expect the Minister of Customs to be here in a few moments. I have no quarrel with the statement just made by my hon. friend. When we began going into this automobile question I discovered for the first time-and it was also a surprise to the present Minister of Customs-that that method had prevailed for some years under previous governments. They made this arrangement; they had a ruling on it, and some of them had a discount of as much as 35 per cent. It was not only the dealers, but we discovered that some of the manufacturers were taking advantage of that and were bringing in cars and reselling them.

That is the
fault of the customs.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Surely; I will admit that at
once; I will admit that that should not prevail. It is not fair.

I have heard
of similar cases. For instance,, we have a Jaw on our statute books providing for the

goods to be entered at the fair market value on the other side. How do they find out the fair market value? They do it by making a sale to somebody. In other words, a manufacturer in, the United States will go to New York and give a whole district comprising three or four states to one firm; they will make that firm responsible for the district and give them the outside discount. That is the discount used, to come into Canada, and these very people, by means of what the minister describes as fake companies, are allowed to sell these cars at 20 per cent off another list. On the very face of it that shows that the customs is being robbed, but how on earth the minister can blame the Canadian manufacturer for this same thing I cannot understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not blame the Canadian manufacturer.

I am speaking
of the Minister of Customs. How he can conclude from that that the Canadian manufacturer is to blame for this condition is something I cannot understand. The Minister of Finance told us he did not want to injure either the automobile manufacturer or the manufacturer of parts, that in fact what he wanted to do was to have more cars and more parts made in this country, and he was going to accomplish that by this reduction. And he said that in respect to the Cadillac car he expected to have them or their parts made here. That shows at once that the minister and his advisers do not know the question at all. The Cadillac car, in the quantities used in this country, could not be made here; it is an absolute economic impossibility. This is not the kind of car that can be made in Canada. The duty on these cars should be kept higher, because they are for the rich people who can afford to pay and should pay for them. Nothing can be done by this or any other government to have that car manufactured in Canada.
I am not an automobile manufacturer, but I have something to do with the parts business and I know something about it. The minister says that he is not going to hurt the parts people at all, and he would like to know how he is doing so. First of all, as I pointed out before, in order to conserve this parts business, you must have the automobile industry conserved; the parts people are simply out of luck if the automobiles come in from the United States as such. How can you expect me, as a manufacturer, to supply a rim or a wheel or a hub or any other part of that car if the car comes into

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
Canada fully manufactured? It cannot be done. Now the minister brings in a new resolution in respect to wheels and parts of cars. We have not reached it yet, but in it the duty is made a little higher than on the finished car. That is not practical.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a drawback of 25
per cent.

But even if that is taken off, this is worth nothing. In other words, everyone knows that you cannot charge a higher rate of duty on the parts than on the finished car. That is unbusinesslike and impracticable, and I will show the minister why, under his very resolution. Let us assume that 50 per cent is made by the automobile manufacturer in the way of the body, the chassis, the frame, or otherwise. Then he sets out to buy the other parts of the car. There are some small accessories that must be brought in. The manufacturer of the car looks around to see where he cam get his parts. He has to buy his wheel, he may have to buy his engine, and may have to buy the body and top. Some manufacturers make these and then buy the remainder of the car. He comes to me as a wheel manufacturer, and what does he say? He says, "If I import those wheels from the United States I can bring them in on that duty less 25 per cent. How much can you save me of this duty?" Now that is the business end of it. These wheels have to be supplied, therefore, at less than the American price plus the duty, saving the manufacturer of cars probably one-half the duty. I ask the minister, what good to me is the 20 per cent tariff on wheels? It is not worth a snap of the finger.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surely my
hon. friend does not argue that he must sell the wheel at the American price plus half the duty or he will not get the business? He does not contend that the Canadian manufacturer would force him into that position?

The hon. minister has not been in the business and does not know the practical side of it. In the first place, every one of the manufacturers are exporters of wheels. We as manufacturers of wheels, or of the bodies or tops or anything else, try to get as much of that export business as we can, and by getting the rebates of duty we must, if we want the business, meet the American price. Having done so on part of the export business, they say to us, "Now we have given you so much of the export business you are able to make your whole article for less money, we expect you to do it, and we are doing it by means of the export 14011-232J
business and the volume of trade." You could not do it otherwise, and if by any chance any of the export business is lost to us we could not make the article that we are making, even at the price we are. It is impossible to do it. I do not know whether I have made that clear or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I do not follow my hon. friend.

As a matter
of fact the process is this: when we make goods and the American manufacturer comes over here he says to us, "You must show us some reason why we should not buy these goods in the United States. If we buy them in the United States we pay a certain rate of duty, but on that wheel we are making in the United States we have a profit, and if we give that business to you we lose the profit we are making in the United States," so that we have got to come down below the American price plus the Canadian duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before we get too far away
from the observations of my hon. friend, who is in the business and understands it, I may say I was impressed with his argument when he first started. He quoted the case of a car similar to the Cadillac and said it was impossible that that type of car could be made profitably in Canada, and for that reason we should put on a higher duty.
Not on account of the type of car, but on account of the quantity of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He said that they could not
be built in Canada, and for that reason we should keep up the tariff and get the revenue. I do not agree with my hon. friend, but he is in the business and knows better than I do.

I am not in
the business. That is my own personal opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is right,
why not take off the duty altogether and put on an excise tax of 50 per cent; then the government would get all the revenue? I do not say my hon. friend's argument is right, but if it is, why should we not do as I suggest?

That is for
the government to decide. I have given my own opinion. So far as that particular car is concerned, the only work you get out of it if you bring it into Canada in parts is the assembling cost. But the hon. minister knows right well, and the gentleman sitting

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
in front of him can tell him, what the assembling cost of a car is. It is a very very small item, and if it is to assemble the car only, I simply say that so far as the employment of labour goes it does not amount to a hill of beans.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend. I believe Canadians can do this work as well as they can in the United States, and it is to their advantage to manufacture in Canada because of the export business. They would not get the advantages they have in Canada if they were shipping from the United States. I will admit at once that they are under a little handicap because of the fair market value in the country of origin. If they get their fair market value down a little lower in Canada they will be in a more advantageous position to export. I know that the fly in the ointment was the clause providing that they must manufacture 50 per cent in Canada, but some of them had frankly admitted that they had no objection to that. Another matter which I have not mentioned before is that for the first year we are going to put them on a 40 per cent basis in Canada and give them up to March 31 next year to get up to the 50 per cent basis. That will give them leeway enough, and I have the assurance of the automobile men-Mr. Russell and Mr. McLaughlin; I forget the other gentleman's name, representing one of the other companies-that they think they can come to that figure within that period. I am told the Ford people are over that; they are quite satisfied and are not finding any fault. The policy of the government is to encourage the additional manufacture of these goods in Canada, and we believe this measure will help us.

The minister has confidence that Canadians can do this work. So have I. But they cannot work against impossibilities. They cannot manufacture a few cars of a certain type at any cost on the basis of which they can sell them. Surely that must be clear. No matter what the minister does; whether he makes it 50, 60 or 70 per cent, we are not going to make this range of high priced cars in this country. The tooling cost of one of those cars is so immense that it would never pay to make them in Canada. The matter is one of dollars and cents. To put out an absolutely new model car the tooling cost is more than half a million dollars. If you spread that over a thousand cars made on this side, what do you have? You have an impossible proposition at once. Such a car can never be made in Canada and if the minister has any expectations along that 
line he is going to be disappointed. Any arrangements made regarding the smaller car are sound, but any arrangements regarding the higher priced cars are absolutely unsound. I would not undertake to make a wheel for a car like the Cadillac. You would not get your tooling cost out of the profits on it in five years. What applies to that article will apply to every other article about the car.
If that be the case why does my hon. friend object to allowing those cars to come into Canada at a reasonable rate of duty?

On those high priced cars I think the rate of duty should be as high as it can be placed. A man who can afford to buy a Cadillac or any other car at $4,000 or $5,000 should be taxed to the limit.
^Mr. BOIVIN: That man is already taxed 27i per cent of the value of his car plus a 5 per cent sales tax, a 5 per cent excise tax on $1,200 and a 10 per cent excise tax on the balance over $1,200. What more protection does the hon. member advocate for a high priced car?

As regards
luxuries I would impose a tax as high as possible. They were brought in under a duty of 35 per cent and people who can afford to buy a high priced car will import it even if the duty is 50 per cent.
Then my hon. friend gets away entirely from his argument of protection.
The question is one of revenue, not protection at all.
This is the first time that I have heard my hon. friend agree with us that the tariff should be for revenue and not only for protection.
I never argued that.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen are very easily pleased, but if they will look over my addresses in this House on the French treaty they will find that I have advocated consistently a duty as high as possible on all imported luxuries. A high priced car is a luxury if there ever was one. There is not a bit of protection in such a duty.

Surely there is an element of protection. If you raise the duty to 75 or 100 per cent you are going to force a certain number of people in Canada to buy cars

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
manufactured in this country. Those who can afford it will pay the higher rate of duty, but those who cannot will buy cars manufactured in Canada.
I shall be glad to answer my hon. friends opposite when they can agree amongst themselves. One argues that it is tariff for revenue only-
Nobody argues that.
1 heard that argument of my hon. friend from Lincoln just a few moments ago.
The minister misinterpreted it. Mr. CLARK: The minister did not hear all the argument this evening.
I am sorry I was not here early enough to hear the whole argument, but if I wait to read it in Hansard I shall have to wait until to-morrow afternoon.
The hon. member understands perfectly what I mean. I give him credit for more common sense than he is trying to make out he has.

I should like to ask the Minister of Customs the question I asked the Minister of Finance a few minutes ago. The Minister of Customs stated this afternoon- and his confreres nearly smashed the tops of their desks in applauding his statement- that -Canadian manufacturers were selling their automobiles in foreign countries at a lower price than they were selling them in Canada less the drawback, sales tax and all other taxes. That means that the manufacturers were exploiting Canadian consumers. I should like to ask him now to give us the details, the price of any particular car he wishes after deducting all the taxes, and the price that it is sold at in this country and any other country he likes.
I am afraid my hon. friend did not exactly understand me this afternoon.
I understand the minister perfectly.

I said that for the purpose of my argument I was willing to eliminate the sales tax and the excise tax. It is well understood by all of us that the sales tax and the excise tax are not collected on cars exported. I further said that when a car manufactured in Canada is exported to a foreign country, the Canadian manufacturer charges a lesser rate than he charges in Canada and the difference in the rate is the amount of the drawback which he receives on the United States parts and materials
which go into that- car. I have tried to follow and carry out my argument by saying that if parts upon which at the present time a duty is paid and a drawback given should oome in free and if other parts should come in with a reduction in duty, the Canadian consumer can get the benefit of that reduction just as well as the consumer in New Zealand, Australia or any other country to which those cars are exported. In every case the same amount of Canadian labour is used and the same wages are paid. reduce the price of the car to the Canadian consumer. If my hon. friend wants me to tell him the exact difference in price in regard to any particular make of car I will admit frankly I have not that information before me. I am glad that my hon.

I was merely asking the

Section 42 of that act
reads:
If any difficulty arises in determining the fair market value for duty of goods imported into Canada, which are the manufacture or production of foreign countries or Great Britain, such as musical instruments, sewing-machines, agricultural machines or implements, medical preparations, commonly called patent medicines, and other goods, the prices of which are published iby the manufacturers or producers, or persons acting on their behalf, the governor in council may, from time to time, fix and determine a certain rate of discount which may be applied to such published prices of any such manufactures or productions, and such published prices, subject to deduction of the amount of discount according to such rate, shall be deemed and taken to be the fair market values of any such manufactures or productions respectively as are specified in such order in council.
That is the authority and I interpret it as a provision intended to prevent abuses. It was never the intention of that clause to enable any government to decide by order in council that the duty should be collected on the retail price of an article, and so long as I remain Minister of Customs the clause shall never be so interpreted. If however I do find that there is abuse, if I find that any American corporation is bringing cars into the country on a 35 per cent discount and then disposing of them, to the Canadian dealer at a discount of only 20 per cent, I shall ask my colleagues to pass an order to ensure that they pay the duty on the price of the car, less the discount they give to the Canadian dealer.

The idea is to prevent

Yes.

With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and which has been discussed a good deal this evening, I hold here a piece of specific information which I think I should submit to the committee. It is an article taken from the Lethbridge Herald of April 27, 1926. The Lethbridge Herald is, I think, a reliable paper, and under the caption "Protection that protects" it states editorially:
It is little wonder that Canadian motor car manufacturers have been wailing loudly about some of their protection being taken away from them: why shouldn't they when an Oshawa-made automobile which costs $2,090 in Oshawa, can be bought for $1,295 at Nassau in t-he Bahamas, British West Indies?
Gerald A. Sweeting, now living in Toronto, who formerly lived in Nassau, ordered a 5-passenger McLaughlin sedan there. He could have bought it for $1,295. In explaining how this $800 difference in a $1,295 car comes about, the factory officials explain that there is a 5 per cent sales tax and a 10 per cent luxury tax which are not paid on the export cars.
It is also pointed out that, to 'help the export trade, a 90 per cent drawback of the duty on imported parts is allowed. But with these figures in mind, the general public will still be left with the impression that the Oshawa manufacturers will be able to get along very nicely with 27$ per cent protection on higher priced cars as against the old import duty of 35 per cent.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the old saying is that where there is smoke there is fire. It is not always true, but generally it is.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member for East Essex laughs, but when so many intelligent people in this country are firmly convinced from their own knowledge and from the knowledge of their friends that certain articles, highly protected in Canada, are sold in foreign markets at lower prices than are available to the domestic consumer, there is some reason for their contention that the duty should be reduced so that Canadians should not be compelled to pay higher prices for a Canadian product than those at which it is sold to people in other countries. No, no.

But this car was made in the same factory.
I tell my hon. friend that they make a different car for every market.

speechtext: If you will permit me, Mr. Chairman, I quite appreciate that you want to be fair with us all, and that your ruling is intended to expedite business, but inasmuch as items 438a and 438b are automobile items, may I suggest that you allow pretty wide latitude in this discussion?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think some hon.
members are jumping too hastily to conclusions. I did not make any ruling as tc what should be discussed. All I called attention to was the fact that we are discussing this particular item, and that we should endeavour to keep as closely to it as possible. I think the committee will agree that I have given as wide latitude as possible, both yesterday and again to-day, and I intend still to do so. But we must not get too far away from the item under discussion and repeat matters that have already been discussed, and pretty well decided, on previous items.

If you will remember,
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Customs was not in the House when the hon. member for Lincoln first brought this matter up, and it was remarked that when he came in he would answer it.

I agree entirely with your
interpretation of the rules, Mr. Chairman, but as the question has been asked, I would not like to have it appear that the minister was unable to answer it. So I hope the committee will be indulgent and allow the answer to be given, and then wye can take up the next item in the regular way.
If I understood the question correctly, my hon. friend asked me to give the name of some specific car that came in in this way, or of some specific car where the Canadian manufacturer got the same protection, or the -improper protection, that I have pointed out.

If the minister will allow me to interrupt, he is very skilfully putting my question in his own way. I prefer very much to put my question in my own way. The minister gives the House a hypothetical case of a car being brought in from the other side. I do not question that; I believe that it can be established. Now I ask him, in view of the fact that he said the Canadian car was taking advantage of a similar price for a similar car, to name a car made in Canada that approximates this car sold at $5,414 36. I asked him to name two cars; I will ask for only one.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

I told my hon. friend that before six o'clock; I gave him the answer. My hon. friend well knows that there are two cars on the market to-day, one, which is supposed to be a Canadian car, known as the Cadillac limousine sedan, which was priced in Canada just previous to the change in duty at $5,600, and the other a Pierce-Arrow seven-passenger limousine sedan. The car imported direct from the United States, costing $3,500 in that country and $5,414.36 here, plus $180 for freight which brings it up to $5,600, is a Pierce-Arrow. The Cadillac limousine sedan, which is supposed to be a Canadian car-I do not know whether it is assembled here or imported from the United States, but it is sold here as a Canadian car-* is sold at exactly the same price as the other American car. They both sell in the United States for $3,500 and in Canada for $5,600.

If the minister will say that either of these cars is a Canadian car in any sense of the word I will admit that he is right. There may be some force to his argument, but neither of these cars can be classed as a Canadian car, and I defy the minister to name one solitary car made in Canada against which company the claim he made a few moments ago can be substantiated.

I wish my hon. friend were so absolutely right every time he defies anyone on this side of the House. He knows very well that I cannot name a Canadian car which is sold in this country at $5,600, because there is no Canadian car made in Canada which is sold at that price. But if my hon. friend wants me to start my calculations all over again and take a $1,200 car or an $1,800 car, he will see that the proportions work out in exactly the same way. The American manufacturer, instead of putting $500 into his pocket on a $5,000 car, will put $100 in his pocket on a $1,000 car.

I wonder if the minister could explain something to me. The price of the Ford coupe in the United States is given as $500, while in Canada, since the new prices have been published it is listed at $625, an increase of $125 or 25 per cent. The Tudor sells in the United States at $520 and in Canada at $650, an increase of 25 per cent, while Fordor sells in the United States at $565, and in Canada at $710, or an increase of 25.6 per cent. The tariff as fixed in the new schedule is only 20 per cent, and yet these cars are sold in Canada at an increase of 25 per cent, 25 per cent and 26.6 per cent respectively over the United States price. Possibly the Minister of Customs can explain that.
Yes, I think I can explain that to my hon. friend. It may be that the published price of the Ford car in Canada includes sales tax and excise tax.

I am quoting from an advertisement appearing in the 'Grain Growers' Guide, which says:
Ail prices at Ford, Ontario, Freight and government taxes extra.

I still think I can explain :t to my hon. friend. The reason is that the American Ford car must be imported by the original purchaser who goes to the United States, buys it, and brings it to Canada. In ether words I am informed that there is a business undertaking between the Ford Motor Company of Detroit, Michigan, and the Ford Motor Company of Ford City, by which the United States company will not sell cars to Canadian dealers, and for that reason the Canadian consumer cannot buy an American Ford car from a Canadian dealer. Therefore the company manufacturing Ford cars in Canada are not obliged to limit their price exactly to the difference in duty; they can afford to charge, and they do charge, a little bit more, because they take advantage of the inconvenience to a Canadian citizen in going to the United States and making a purchase, and of the increased rates of freight the Canadian purchaser would be obliged to pay if he bought his car in the United States. They claim that the Canadian car is of better quality, but that explains the difference between the 20 per cent provided for by the tariff and the 25 per cent difference charged by the Ford Company.
Will the minister admit that instead of having a 20 per cent protection under the new schedule, the automobile men really have a protection amounting to 25 per cent?
Will the minister tell us how much that is? Is it not practically 24 per cent?

No, it is exactly 20 per cent on the retail price of the car. Then there is a. five per cent sales tax on the price of the car jilus the duty and there is a five per cent excise tax on the price of the .car plus the duty as well.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

But is there not in the United States a three per cent excise tax which the buyer of the car must pay? That certainly makes 23 per cent, and the 20 per cent is charged on that total, which makes practically 24 per cent. In addition to that, if a Canadian buys a car in the United States he must provide himself with a license of the state in which he buys the car before he can drive that car out of the United States. So the point I would like to bring out-and if I am wrong I hope the minister will correct me-is that thg manufacturers of these cheaper cars in Canada to-day have a protection of at least 25 per cent.

My hon. friend is certainly right when he says that the individual Canadian consumer going to the United States has to pay a 3 per cent excise tax, and the retail value of that car in the United States is the cost of the car plus the excise tax, so he has to pay duty on that price. When my hon. friend says that aimounts to a protection of 24 per cent or 25 per cent I would hesitate to agree, because I would hardly call protection the amount of excise tax the purchaser is obliged to pay to the United States government before he brings his car across the line. But it means practically what my hon. friend says. The reason Why in my argument a moment ago I did not take into account the excise tax is that when the car is exported from the United States to Canada, the excise tax is not collected by the United States government. It is used for the purpose of determining the retail value of the car for duty purposes, but it is not collected when the car is sold for export from the United States.
By the dealer.

By the dealer or by the
distributor. I think if it were possible for the consumer to prove export of a Ford car from the United States, that tax would not be collected even from the consumer. But I agree with my hon. friend that it is impossible for the purchaser of a Ford car in the United States to prove export of that car, because the Ford dealers in that country are forbidden to sell cars to Canadians. They can buy them as individuals, pay the American excise tax and bring them across the line themselves, but if the Ford dealer knows the car is to be exported to Canada, he is instructed by the Ford Motor Company not to sell it, owing to the agreement existing with the Ford Motor Company of Canada.
I would like to ask the hon. member what class of Ford car he was referring to.
I named them all. I started with a coupe.

Very well; that is a
closed car. I would like to ask the minister if it is not a fact that you must take from the protection which the customs duties give, the duty on imported parts, for instance; the duty on coal, or the duty on steel. Would that not be a fair reduction from the amount of duty which is placed upon the imported article complete?

Oh yes. My hon. friend is quite right when he says that from the protection given on the car we should deduct the duty paid on coal and the duty paid on parts which are necessarily imported from the United States. But I say that with the amendment which was announced by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance just before six o'clock, and which we will reach in a moment, the Ford people will no longer have to pay any duty on any of their parts. They will come in absolutely free, because they are the most complete manufacturing plant in Canada. Everything that is made in Canada is either made by them in their own plant or purchased from a Canadian manufacturer, and all the Ford company imports is the parts which they cannot possibly obtain in Canada. They will derive perhaps more benefit than any other plant from the provision placing parts on the free list, but of course when my hon. friend from Macleod made the statement concerning the Ford car imported by the consumer and made the comparison between the 20 per cent duty mentioned in the tariff and the 20 or 25 per cent absolute protection which the Ford plant had in Canada, he was absolutely right. But that is a special case which relates only to the Ford car.
Would that not apply to the Dodge car, the Buick, and almost any other car assembled in Canada?

Not exactly, because the
Dodge dealers, the Buick dealers and the other dealers in cars assembled in Canada are not bound by contract and there is nothing in any written agreement between the Canadian and the American companies which prohibits Canadian dealers from buying American cars. If the car is bought through a Canadian dealer, it will escape the payment of the 3 per cent excise tax.

Ways and, Means-Customs Tariff

My hon. friend will admit
they will hold the consumer up the same as the Ford people are doing.

I have been arguing all
afternoon that the Canadian consuming public has been held up by these manufacturers-

And also has
made it plain that what he is doing is not making much difference. He laughs, but he knows it is true. The greatest thing behind the agitation has been the Ford car, and anybody who knew anything about it knew the whole situation. It has always been the same, there never was any change. All the different statements about everything being tariff was just so much nonsense. Here we have the exact figures and a confession.
And the complaint is that it is not going to be worth much.
Did my hon. friend say the complaint was that it was not going to be worth much?
The complaint that the duty of 20 per cent is inactive; instead of that there is a duty of 25 per cent.

My hon. friend pointed out to hon. members opposite that the cut in duty was not quite so great as they imagined, but at the same time I think we will all admit that the 25 per cent duty is very much better than the 40 per cent duty which they previously enjoyed.

Just in the
same way, we have lots of things oovered by patent. Our cream separator business is on the same basis. True, we have absolutely no tariff at all on that article; the whole thing is covered by patent right. The best protection for anybody in the world is the patent protection with agreements from the parent company. My hon. friend has been quite interesting to-night. He has been giving us an honest confession. Frauds have been committed on the country and on the customs, and they are continuing. Frauds are being committed with reference to automobiles coming in, on his own statement. Then he refers to bogus companies. He says they are within the law. I do not know that a bogus company can ever be looked upon as being within the law.
Or fake company.
Or fake company.
I may perhaps have used a word I should not have used.

All right, we
will accept that.

moment that the company does not exist. Paying at a
higher value.

Your hon. friend is not defending anyone to-night. I do not know why my hon. friend should say that, unless he wants to draw out some of the arguments which I do not think are at all conclusive which we have been favoured with this afternoon.

He wants to draw out
applause from behind him.

why the clapping does not materialize when he makes that statement. He will have a complaint against his back benchers; they are not running up to form. My hon. friend says this was drawn to his attention by a Canadian manufacturer. I do not wonder at it. I would have thought they would have drawn it to his attention and would have been insistent upon getting rid of it. But he says it is an evil; he does not like the word "fraud."
Fake.

I do not distinguish between fraud and fake. The fact is

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
that the Canadian Customs department have been losing a lot of money which they should not have lost. My hon. friend will agree that if we had in this country a different basis of valuation this fraud or fake could not take place. Am 1 right?

No, I certainly will not
admit my hon. friend is right. He is so seldom right that I do not think he can be right this time.

My hon. friend has answered the question. Is he at all aware of the suggestion-it was more than a suggestion, it was put into legislation-that the valuation for customs purposes should be a valuation based on the cost of production, plus manufacturers' profits and distributing expenses? Is the hon. minister aware of that?
That that request was made?

No, that there
was a provision to that effect.

No, I am not aware that
there is a clause to that effect. I have been told by the officials of my department who have been there for many years administering the Customs Tariff that at one time there was such a clause. It is not in existence now.

The clause was struck out in 1922, rendering it possible for this sort of thing to go on. Instead of making a complaint against the Canadian manufacturers and instead of making a complaint against the tariff with which it has nothing to do, it would have become my hon. friend very much better if he had brought in something to enable him to stop this kind of fake business in Canada, these fake companies, these schemes of beating the customs. I might go back to the valuations which we had in 1921, which would have prevented those frauds, but I suppose that is a course of action that it is idle to seek any progress on from this government.
I want to address myself to the particular item under discussion having regard to it as such and not to its relation to the valuation of motor cars for customs purposes. The Minister of Finance admitted this afternoon that as the processing went on the rate went up. The Minister of Customs did not admit it, but it was a sound argument and I suppose he will admit it.	'
I also admit it.

Then we have both ministers agreeing; we are all agreed on that, and therefore the rate on the parts ought to be always less than the rate on the whole because there is just that much Canadian labour to be looked after as the processing is carried on further and further. The Minister of Customs nods his head. I assume he means that is correct. He again nods his head. Very good. Under those circumstances, I seriously ask the government in view of their own statement: How do they think this item is proper? On parts such as tops, wheels and bodies which are the chief parts that go into automobiles we have rates of 20, 271 and 30 per cent. Of course, the 30 per cent rate is really the one in which we are interested. 1 am quite aware that it is proposed to give a rebate of 25 per cent in connection with that rate. I understand from the Minister of Finance that that is correct. That would reduce the rate of 30 per cent in which we are interested to 22J per cent. Is my hon. friend going to leave it in that way?
Yes.
In other words, against the principle which they laid down, the rates on the parts are to be greater than the rates on the completed article, because that is the effect of this section as I read it.

When the government had the intention of reducing the duty on motor cars from 35 to 271 per cent on the high priced car and from 35 to 20 per cent on the car valued at less than $1,200, those parts that are mentioned in this particular item were not taken into consideration by the government. It was in the minds of the officials of both departments that the intention of the government was to reduce the rates on the parts to absolutely the same rate as that on the motor cars themselves.
That was the old law.

Yes, because under the
original item 438-there was then only one item-an appraisers' bulletin had been issued on the 21st November, 1919, under a ruling of the Board of Customs, that those four component parts, chassis, wheels, tops and bodies, would pay exactly the same rate of duty as the completed car. There were many reasons for that, the principal one being to prevent people from dismantling cars, importing them in portions and then putting them together. Relying upon that old bulle-

IFa?/s and Means-Customs Tariff
tin, the Department of Customs, after consultation with the tariff advisers in the Department of Finan'ce but without referring the matter to the government, issued an appraisers' bulletin on the 17th April, the day after the budget came down. The bulletin reads as follows:
In conformity with the ruling in appraisers' bulletin No 2018, tops, wheels, chassis or completed bodies, for use on automobiles or motor trucks, are rated under tariff item 438a and 438b.
Those articles are to be rated under tariff item 438b only when the following certificate is subscribed to on the face of the sworn to entry; otherwise, they are to be rated under tariff item 438a.
Then the bulletin contains the form of a certificate which is to be signed by persons importing those- parts for the cheaper cars. When that bulletin was issued parts makers from all parts of Canada came to Ottawa and asked the government to do something to meet their needs and requirements, pointing out that if the duty on their parts was reduced to 20 per cent and if, in addition to that 20 per cent, there was to be a 25 per cent drawback on the same parts when imported from the United States to be placed in cars the content of which was 50 per cent or more Canadian, they could not remain in business. They interviewed the Minister of Finance; many of them came to see me; they saw nearly all the members of the government. It was explained to them very frankly-and this is the only change that is being made now in the budget and it is not a substantial change-that we intended that the duties on parts would remain as they were, but that they would be reduced by 25 per cent when the parts were imported from the United States to go into Canadian made cars. Parts men and automobile manufacturers met and in their meetings-and one of those meetings took place in my room- they came to the understanding that the duty on parts should be reduced to 30 per cent. The present tariff is 35 per cent and the reduction is therefore from 35 to 30 per cent. My hon. friend says that there is only one thing wrong; that it would be perfect if that rate was not higher than the duty on cars; that as the part is a component part of the entire automobile, the duty should be less instead of more. The duty is not less, but it is also not more and I am going to show my hon. friend how that happens. He saw the point at once and he admitted a moment ago that this 30 per cent was subject to a 25 per cent drawback which reduced the rate to 22J per cent. The part makers told us that
it was absolutely impossible to have two rates on parts; that the same material entered into the wheels, bodies and tops, and that they would prefer a uniform rate.
That is right.
On the average.
Yes.
Cars are not sold on the average.

But still we must meet the demands of the parts manufacturers and try to meet their wishes by finding an average. That is the plan which they proposed to us. They said: Seeing that you are going to impose a uniform rate on parts, we would like to have you average the rate on the parts to the average rate on the cars sold. The average rate on cars will be 22J per cent and the average rate on parts will be absolutely the same.

Does the Minister of
Customs consider tires a part of a car?
Yes.
What duty is now assessed on tires?
The duty on tires at the present time is 35 per cent, but I am glad to say that there is no tire factory in Canada to-day taking advantage of the full protection.

The minister said that there would be no higher duty on parts imported for further manufacture. Any Canadian manufacturer importing tires or any part which bears 35 per cent duty-and there are many such parts-will now have a protection of 27^ per cent, w'hereas if I, say, want to import a car carrying tires or parts of the same value, I shall have to pay a duty of 20 per cent. I do not think the minister can question the truth of this statement. In other words, the minister in this budget says to me: "If you want to buy a Canadian car I am going to charge you 27J per cent on every American
366S

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
part that enters into the manufacture of that car; 'but if you import an American car made by American labour I will charge you, in respect of those parts, only 20 per cent." Is not that the situation?
Is my hon. friend anxious to reduce the duty on tires to 20 per cent?

No, but I am anxious to have the matter scientifically investigated. Andl to prove my contention that it has not been studied on that basis I will quote two observations made by the Minister of Finance this afternoon. In the first place he declared that he was bewildered when confronted by the manufacturers with their problems, and then he talked about having to grope around to find a solution for certain difficulties. These two admissions alone constitute a sufficient evidence that diue investigation has not been made into this industry. I do not pose as an expert on the automobile question, but I am asking for fair treatment for the industry and I claim that it is unfair to expect a Canadian manufacturer to compete with American producers when we levy a duty of 27| per cent on parts imported by him while every other Canadian citizen is encouraged to go to the United States and buy a finished car on which he will pay only 20 per cent in respect to these particulars parts.
When my hon. friend makes a plea for the tire manufacturers of Canada-

I am not making a plea for the tire manufacturers or for anyone else. I want the minister to understand that I am speaking in behalf of the industry as a whole, and particularly in the interests of the workmen. The great bulk of the automobile manufacturers are Americans who have branch factories here, and so far as they are concerned it is not a matter of very much moment to them if you do kill the industry in Canada, because in a very few months, almost anyone could absorb the capital lost in the Canadian factories. But my point is that for the sake of the tremendous pay-roll and of our Canadian people who are employed in the industry, the matter is one that should be scientifically investigated and not left to the decision of a government which has to grope around in a bewildered state.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have had a fair discussion of this item and I think the committee is satisfied that we are trying to deal fairly with all industries. I suggest that we might now pass the item and proceed with the three

I mentioned at six o'clock. We could clean up this sheet and get through, seeing that many hon. gentlemen are anxious to catch the train.

The minister has said that in New Zealand the regulations provide that for duty purposes the assessment shall be made on the fair market value in the country of origin, and he went on to suggest that it would be advantageous to Canada to adopt the same principle here. I would ask him, first, whether he proposes to make a. change in the present valuations for duty purposes; and, secondly, what in his opinion is the difference between the principle applied in New Zealand and that applied in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why should we go over that ground again to-inight? The Minister of Customs explained the point fully.
The Minister of Finance made the statement a moment ago that the duty of 20 per cent would be assessed on the retail value of the car. Is the duty so assessed to-diay?

At the present time the duty on a car imported by the ultimate consumer who buys it in the United States is assessed on the retail value, but in respect of all cars imported from the United States by dealers or distributors-and my hon. friend will readily recognize the difference between a dealer and a distributor-the duty is charged, not on the retail, but on the wholesale price.
Charged to whom?
To the distributor, if imported by him.
On the first sale from the manufacturer.
On the first sale from the manufacturer to the distributor, and if it is imported by a dealer he also is entitled to a discount.
In what way does that differ from the practice established in New Zealand now?

When goods are imported into New Zealand the value for duty is calculated on the retail value in the country of origin. At the present time they have a duty of 10 per cent on cars imported from Canada as against a duty of 25 per cent on cars imported from the United States. As the Minister of Finance pointed out this afternoon, every time we do anything by our tariff to reduce the retail value of motor cars manufactured in

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
this country we are giving an advantage to our manufacturers in the New Zealand market by widening the difference between the duty paid by our manufacturers and that paid by their United States competitors.

Does the Minister of Customs
agree with the Minister of Finance that the New Zealand system would be preferable to the one in vogue here?

I was not present when the hon. Minister of Finance referred to that matter. I am not sure that he made the statement, because I know that our automobile manufacturers have for the last month been asking him to incorporate that system in our tariff and make the duty payable on the full retail value of the car. So far as I know he has not granted their request.
(Mr. CLARK: He stated this afternoon that in his opinion it would be advisable.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated this afternoon that the New Zealand method was worth considering in view of the situation that had developed in Canada of a 35 per cent discount.

Mr. Chairman, how can you ever expect to be able to export Canadian cars to New Zealand under present conditions, where you have your excise tax that enlarges the retail value of your car, with the result that New Zealand imposes a disj criminating duty .because of that very enlargement of price? You never can do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is trying to induce me to lose some of my excise tax.
No, I am stating *what is a fact. While that excise tax is continued you absolutely prevent the export of Canadian cars to New Zealand.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is very much to be said for that view.
Does the Minister of Customs think the government has power under section 42 of the Customs Act to change the basis of valuation for duty by order in council?

The hon. member for Fort William asked me that question early in the evening, and I answered him that we had never discussed the matter around the council table, but that my own interpretation of section 42 and that of my officers was to the effect that we could not take advantaget of the section to impose the retail price as the value for duty; that we could only apply the section 14011-233
to prevent abuses, for instance, to prevent a subsidiary distributing company from obtaining a higher rate of discount than it could legitimately obtain when cars were merely passing through its hands to be sold to other dealers.

May I point out that in 1924 this government did pass an order in council in connection with agricultural implements under which they changed the basis of valuation for duty? That order in council provided that the American manufacturer must invoice his goods and pay duty on the basis of the price payable by the American purchaser.- So apparently the government have recognized that they have such power and have actually practised it in the past.

If my hon. friend and those who surround him advocate that we should pass an order in council obliging any Canadian dealer importing an American car to pay duty on the full American retail value, I promise to give his request very serious consideration and to bring it to the attention of my colleagues in council. Possibly if it is within the law, and if everybody on the other side of the House desires that it should be done, it may be done, because it will make absolutely no difference whatever in the cost of the car to the Canadian consumer. What we are endeavouring to do by these changes in the tariff is to lift the load off the shoulders of the Canadian consumer by bringing down the price of motor cars.

I would have thought in view of what my hon. friend said to-day that he would want to stop fraud on the customs and secure proper valuations, irrespective of whether the act covers it or not. I would have thought that he would consider it his duty to see that proper valua-1 tions are made and render impossible fraud on the customs of this country by (fake companies. All such frauds ought to be stopped now.

I said this afternoon that if my hon. friends on the other side would allow me to remain Minister of Customs a little while longer I would recommend to council the passing of an order whereby no importer of cars would be allowed to claim an unreasonable discount upon the list price of the car imported to evade the payment of fair duty.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is another one-

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the Minister of Customs very emphatically stated, and a few minutes ago the Minister of Finance also stated, that neither wanted the excise tax to be touched. In other words, they wanted this money for the purpose of paying off the war debt. I wonder if it has ever occurred to some other hon. gentlemen-I know it has to those ministers -just how much is now being taken off the revenue of the country by lowering the price of automobiles. Eleven per cent of the cars used in Canada are imported. Those cars used to pay 35 per cent; they are now going to pay 20 per cent. Two out of every three of them will pay 20 per cent, the balance will pay 27i per cent. Besides this, the price of all cars being lowered, the excise tax and the sales tax will be reduced upon the total amount of sales. Furthermore, the duty on parts that are imported is cut to 20 per cent in some cases, and many will be admitted free, which again will reduce the revenue very seriously. If hon. gentlemen opposite had taken the easy way and removed 5 or 10 per cent from the sales tax, instead of upsetting the whole country by these changes, I wonder if they would not have arrived at exactly the same result. What is going to happen now, with some exceptions, is that we are going to get a slightly cheaper motor car at the expense of the national revenue. The minister shakes his head, but that is the fact. Further than that, all these parts were absolutely parts upon which the tariff for revenue-much lauded by my friends across the way-applied, because none were manufactured in this country, such as horns, distributors, ammeters, instrument board lamps, oil gauges, gasolines gauges, thermostats, oil filters, carbureters, and so forth. That is taken out of the revenue of the country; there is nothing else for it. It is a straight reduction of the revenue of the country for
[Mr. Boivin.l
the purpose of reducing the price of automobiles. But it does more than that. Many of these items undoubtedly have been gone over by the experts, and it is only unfortunate that they were not gone over by the experts before the budget was brought down, instead of afterwards. It would have saved the government and the country a great deal of trouble and anxiety. There is this point. Some of these parts are new; they have just been put on cars recently, and there has been no chance for a Canadian manufacturer to develop an industry in these parts. This absolutely precludes the possibility of Canadian manufacturers entering into their manufacture.

My hon. friend loses sight
of the fact that the moment any one of these parts is manufactured in Canada, it comes off the free list, and the duty presently paid on these parts goes on automatically. These parts will be free from duty only so long as they are not manufactured in this country. My hon. friend need not worry, because, after all, the duty paid by automobile manufacturers on these parts averages only about four dollars per *car. We are giving this reduction to the. automobile manufacturer to compensate him in part for the reduction of the duty, the advantage of which we are passing on to the Canadian consumer. I repeat, the duty paid on all these parts that cannot be manufactured in this country at the present time amounts to an average of $4 per car and possibly $8 on the higher priced cars.

I do not know what is
the exact amount, but we will admit that it is $4 per oar. That means just that amount taken from the revenue of the country for the purpose of reducing the price of automobiles. The minister must admit that we shall not receive the same amount of duty per car imported into Canada as before, and 11 per cent of the cars used1 in Canada were imported up until a short time ago. So is not this going to reduce the amount of revenue you are going to receive?

If my hon. friend desires
to have us collect the largest possible amount of duty on cars imported into Canada, we have been wasting our time arguing here this afternoon and this evening. I thought my hon. friend was not anxious that cars be imported into Canada. I thought he wanted them manufactured in this country.

That is what. I want.

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
Then why base his argument on the loss of revenue on cars imported into this country?

That is very simple. I
have known the Minister of Customs for a long time, and I know that he can wiggle out of almost anything. But the fact remains that if you lower the duty to 20 per cent you are going to have more cars imported.

Then there will be more
revenue.
Yes, and fewer cars manufactured in Canada. You cannot eat your cake and have it.
Seeing that my hon. friend has made his speech and my own, there is nothing left to be said.
Item agreed to.

I do not know whether my
hon. friend was out a moment ago when I explained that.
Oh, it is just the 40 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

A few minutes
ago the Minister of Customs told us about the strenuous efforts he made and the time he had with the parts makers in order to bring their condition on a livable basis. He told us that the duty was adjusted, not on the basis of 20 per cent, but it was fixed at 30 per cent, 27^ per cent and 20 per cent on the parts of cars. I want to ask the minister, does he expect that the articles mentioned there will have the protection he speaks of, even less the 25 per cent of rebate, in the event of their being used by manufacturers of cars
14011-233i
who make the 50 per cent? Does he think, for instance, that a manufacturer of tops or bodies will have the benefit of that duty?

I am not sure that the
manufacturer of tops, wheels and bodies in this country will be able to take advantage of the full 30 per cent. That will depend a great deal upon internal competition. That is the argument that is used by my hon. friends on the other side all the time, that if you put the duty high enough, you will have so many factories making the same line of goods that competition will keep prices down. That may be; I am not prepared' to argue against that tonight, but I do not exactly get the point that my hon. friend wants to make, and I would like to explain to him anything I possibly can, if I understand it myself. He says that by giving a protection of 30 per cent to the manufacturers of tops, wheels and bodies, the manufacturers will not get the 30 per cent.

Not at all.
_ Mr. BOIVIN:	I admit that; I admitted
it a little while ago. They will be getting 30 per cent less the 25 per cent of the duty provided in the drawback clause. That will reduce their protection to 22J, per cent.
Does the minister think that they will get the 22J per cent? That is what my question is.

It is a trade
condition. My hon. friend must know it.
That is what I say. I say that if they do not get that full protection it will not be the fault of parliament.
Oh yes.
It is partly the fault of the 25 per cent rebate.

There are a great many
arguments that can be used against the 25 per cent rebate, and the principal argument used by the parts manufacturers is that every one who makes a car in Canada the material entering into the manufacture of which will be at least 60 per cent Canadian can go to each individual Canadian parts maker and say: "The part you are selling to me is the part that makes up the difference in my car between the 50 per cent and the 60 per cent Canadian content. You must sell

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
that part to me at 25 per cent reduction on duty paid on an American part or I shall buy it from the United States." Then he can go to some other part manufacturer and use the same argument with him. I am willing to admit, and I think the Minister of Finance will admit, that this drawback clause is almost tantamount to reducing the duty on parts to 22J per cent. But it has this additional advantage. It will prohibit people from importing all their parts from the United States and using Canada .simply for assembling plants to get the benefit of Canadian prices on their shipments overseas. It will oblige them to manufacture their cars in Canada. There is that advantage to the 25 per cent drawback; there are those who are assembling in Canada at present, such as the Dodge Brothers and the Durant people and others, who are not putting 50 per cent of Canadian content into their cars. Some manufacturers came to us and assured us that they wanted to develop their plants in Canada, and this 40 per cent provision is made to enable them to do so during the next year.

There is one
mistake the minister makes; he should refrain from mentioning names, because he does an injustice to the manufacturers. He mentioned the Durant plant, for example; I can tell him that already the Durant people make more than 50 per cent of their car in Canada, consequently they should not be referred to as people who are making less than that percentage here. What the minister says may be true in respect to others but it is an injustice to this particular firm.

If I have doiTe any injustice to the Durant people, I withdraw the name at once and apologize most sincerely. If they are making more than 50 per cent of their cars in Canada at present, I am glad to be so advised and I hasten to add:	All
honour to them for it.
I know whereof I speak.
I am sure the hon. member is right.

The Minister
of Customs has put his finger on the one thing this government is sure of and the one thing I think they are relying on as the reason why the manufacture of cars must continue in this country. I refer to the British preference, and other preferences with the British dominions. They must continue manufacturing, as he points out, in order to sell in these export markets, and I think there is a great

deal in what he says. But so far as the parts manufacturer is concerned I do not think my hon. friends quite realize the condition. In addition to what has been already stated we have a very large proportion of our business which is export business, calling for refunds. Take the case of a man manufacturing parts with a 50 per cent export business and a 50 per cent local business. What is the effect there? It is to cut down the duty to practically half. He buys for his output, and he knows what proportion of his business is export, so it works out to about 50 per cent net real protection to the part manufacturer.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just before the item passes- and I will hasten, because I know hon. gentlemen want to catch the train-I was rather pleased that the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) reminded my junior colleague that we should be careful in this House in advertising different companies. It now gives me an opportunity of saying to him what I did not like to say earlier in the evening. It occurred to me that he was doing an injury to a certain industry in this country when he said certain cars could not be manufactured in Canada at all. I will tell hon. gentlemen why I mention that. While I was in Australia, trying to negotiate as favourable a trade agreement as I possibly could, the Australians said to us, "We cannot give you a preference on automobiles; you do not manufacture them in Canada; they are all United States concerns." So we should all keep in mind as members of parliament, whatever views we may have, that to say we cannot do things in this country injures our trade.

I think the
minister is inclined to be fair. It was not I who first mentioned the name of a company; I have absolutely refrained from mentioning company names. The minister mentioned that name first, as Hansard will show, and I stated that cars of that description and category could not be made in this country economically. I make that statement now; I am not afraid to repeat it, because I know it is absolutely correct.

I do not like my hon. friend to get away with that. I do not want to start another argument but if you will look at Hansard to-morrow you will find that when I discussed the price of automobiles and the duty upon them, I took as an example a S3,500 car. I said that I referred to no particular make; I refused to mention any names, and it was only after I had been repeatedly urged and questioned by the hon. member,

Importation oj Celery
who asked me to give the name of any particular car in Canada selling at that price, that I told him there was a car in Canada known as the Cadillac that did sell at approximately this figure.
That is perfectly true; I asked that question, but the minister gave me the names of two cars which are made in the United States and not in Canada. He did not answer my question at all.
Then I did no harm to any Canadian company.
